title: The item that came back
teaches: Versions and vector clocks, merging conflicting writes, CRDTs and collaborative editing, consistency models, and CAP and PACELC
summary: **Concurrent writes need a merge rule.** A store that accepts writes on two replicas at once will hold two versions of a key, and it must say what happens next.
**Last writer wins loses writes.** It keeps the version with the later timestamp, throws the other away without a word, and trusts clocks that can be wrong.

**Vector clocks tell newer from concurrent.** One counter per replica, compared entry by entry: if every entry is at least as large the version is newer, and if each is larger somewhere they are concurrent.
**A merge must keep removes as well as adds.** Dynamo's cart merged by union, so a deleted item could come back; an observed-remove set keeps both kinds of change.
**CRDTs merge without asking anyone.** Data types built so that every merge order gives the same result: counters, sets, maps and text, paid for in extra metadata.
**Shared editing works on letters, not positions.** Operational transformation rewrites each edit's position against edits made at the same time; a text CRDT gives every letter a fixed id.
**Name the consistency you offer.** Linearizable, causal, read-your-writes and eventual promise different things, and each feature needs the weakest that is still correct.

**CAP is about partitions.** While replicas cannot reach each other, each must refuse requests or answer without the others; PACELC adds that without a partition the trade is latency against consistency.

blocks.text: The Dynamo paper that lesson 12 followed, presented at SOSP in October 2007, contains a sentence most papers would have left out. When two versions of a customer's cart conflict, the cart service merges them, and "using this reconciliation mechanism, an add to cart operation is never lost. However, deleted items can resurface." A customer removes a book, the book comes back, and Amazon decided that was better than refusing the customer's next click.

The book comes back because of how lesson 12's design accepts writes. During a partition, or simply when two writes arrive at two coordinators at the same moment, two replicas of one key each accept a different change. When they next talk, each holds a version the other has not seen. Any store that takes writes on more than one replica at a time faces this, and it must answer two questions: how to tell whether one version replaced the other, and if neither did, what to keep.

The figure plays one such moment. The cart holds a book. The customer's phone adds a kettle through replica X while the customer's laptop, at almost the same moment, removes the book through replica Y, and X and Y cannot reach each other. Then the partition heals. Four rules for merging the two versions give four different carts.

blocks.caption: One cart, two replicas, a partition. The phone [[adds a kettle|write]] through X and the laptop removes the book through Y; when the partition heals, each replica sends its version to the other and merges by the rule chosen under "Merge by": last writer wins (each replica stamps its write with its own clock), keep both (vector clocks), union, or add and remove sets. Messages move in slow motion.
blocks.task: Try each rule, and find the one that gives the cart the customer meant.

blocks.text: The simplest rule stamps each write with the time on the replica's clock and, when two versions meet, keeps the one with the later stamp. It needs no extra metadata and always gives one answer, which is why Cassandra uses it for every column. In the figure, Y's remove was stamped 30 ms after X's add, so Y's whole cart wins and the kettle disappears. Nothing reports the loss.

Two things go wrong. The rule throws away one of two concurrent writes, every time, so it is right only where the later write really should replace the earlier one, such as a user setting a profile picture. And "later" is read off clocks on different machines. Clocks set by NTP, the Network Time Protocol, which adjusts a machine's clock from time servers over the network, are typically within a few milliseconds of each other and can be off by much more after a fault or a leap second, so the write that happened second can carry the earlier stamp and lose. Lesson 20 shows what it takes to build a clock whose error is known.

In July 1978 Leslie Lamport published "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System" in Communications of the ACM.[^lamport] Its starting point was that machines have no shared clock to agree on, so the order that matters is causal: event a **happened before** event b if a could have influenced b, because they were on one machine in that order or because a message carried news of a to b's machine. Two events where neither happened before the other are **concurrent**, whatever the clocks said.

In 1988 Colin Fidge and Friedemann Mattern each published a way to capture that relation exactly, the **vector clock**. A version carries one counter for each replica that has written it. A replica that accepts a write increases its own counter; a version that merges two takes the larger value of each counter. This lesson writes a clock as each replica's letter followed by its counter, so [X1 Y1] means replica X has counted one write to this key and Y one; a missing letter counts as zero. Comparing two versions is entry by entry:

blocks.title: Comparing two vector clocks
points: Every entry of a is at most the matching entry of b, and one is smaller: a happened before b, and b replaces it. [X1] is before [X2].
Each clock has at least one entry larger than the other's: concurrent. [X2] against [X1 Y1] is concurrent: X counted a write Y never saw, and Y counted one X never saw.
All entries equal: the same version.

blocks.text: Dynamo kept a vector clock with every version. A version whose clock is before another's is dropped. Concurrent versions are all kept, and a read returns them all, called **siblings**, with their clocks. The application merges them and writes the result back with a clock that has seen both, which ends the conflict. In Dynamo's interface a read returns the list of values together with an opaque **context** holding their clocks, and a write passes that context back, which is how the store knows the new value replaces all of them. Pick "Keep both" in the figure to see the two versions handed to the phone. Nothing is lost, but every piece of code that reads a cart must know how to merge one.[^truncation]

The cart service's merge took every item in either version, the **union**. That keeps the kettle and brings back the book, because a version that lacks the book does not say whether the book was never added or was removed. The merge needs to know which. An **observed-remove set** records it: each add carries a tag no other add has, and a remove records the tags of the adds it saw. The merge keeps every add and every remove, and an item is in the set if it has an add whose tag no remove names. The book's add was named by the laptop's remove, so the book stays out; the kettle's add was named by no remove, so the kettle stays in. If the phone had added a second book during the partition, that add's new tag would keep it.

Marc Shapiro, Nuno Preguiça, Carlos Baquero and Marek Zawirski named this family in 2011: **conflict-free replicated data types**, CRDTs. A CRDT's merge gives the same result whatever order updates are merged in (it is commutative and associative) and merging one update twice changes nothing (it is idempotent), so replicas that have received the same updates hold the same value, in whatever order and however many times the updates arrived. The smallest example is a grow-only counter for likes: each replica counts its own likes in its own entry, the total is the sum of the entries, and the merge takes the larger value of each entry, so no like is counted twice or lost.

The cost is metadata and a narrower menu. An observed-remove set keeps a tag for every add and remove, and those can only be cleaned up once every replica is known to have seen them.[^tombstones] Counters, sets, registers, maps and text have CRDT forms; a rule such as "a bank balance may not go below zero" does not, because two replicas can each approve a withdrawal that is fine alone and wrong together.

blocks.title: Choosing a merge rule
points: Last writer wins, where a later write really replaces an earlier one: a profile picture, a setting.
A CRDT, where the data is a counter, a set, a map or text and its merge is clear.
Siblings returned to the application, where only it knows how to merge and no write may be lost.
A single leader (lesson 11), where no merge can be right, such as a balance that must not go below zero.

blocks.text: Shared documents hit the same problem with positions. Each editor applies their own keystrokes at once and sends them to the others, so two edits made at the same moment arrive at each screen in a different order. Positions count from 0, so in "cart" the c is at 0 and the t at 3. An edit named by position, "delete the letter at 3", means a different letter once someone else's insert has shifted the text.

blocks.caption: Alice and Bob both start from "cart". Alice inserts h after the c, Bob deletes the t, and each then receives the other's edit. Pick how edits are sent and applied. Messages move in slow motion.
blocks.task: Apply the edits as sent and watch the two screens disagree, then find a way that makes them agree.

blocks.text: Clarence Ellis and Simon Gibbs described the first answer in 1989 for GROVE, a group outliner at MCC in Austin: **operational transformation**. Before applying a remote edit, rewrite it against every concurrent edit already applied. Alice's insert at position 1 came before position 3, so Bob's delete becomes a delete at 4. Getting the transformations right for every pair of operations and every order of arrival proved hard, and several published algorithms were later shown to diverge. Xerox PARC's Jupiter system in 1995 made it manageable by sending every edit through one central server that fixes the order, so each client transforms only against the server. Google Wave in 2009 and the rewritten Google Docs in 2010 used that design.[^wave]

A **text CRDT** avoids positions altogether. Every letter gets an id when it is typed, made of the editor's id and a counter, and never changes. An insert says which letter it follows and a delete says which letter it removes, so edits mean the same thing in any order, and concurrent inserts at one spot are put in id order, the same on every screen. The price is an id for every letter ever typed, deleted ones included. Libraries such as Automerge and Yjs made this practical for documents of ordinary size.

Evan Wallace described Figma's choice in October 2019. Figma has a central server, as Jupiter did, and a design document is a tree of objects with properties. Two people changing different properties never conflict; two people changing the same property of the same object are settled by **last writer wins**, where "last" is the order the server received them. That loses one of two concurrent changes, but the loser saw the other's change appear a moment later on screen, so nothing vanishes unseen. Figma's post called the design inspired by CRDTs and simpler than them, since the server can decide what peers would otherwise have to agree on.
Every store in the last few lessons promised something about what a read returns, and the promises have names. From strongest to weakest:

blocks.title: Consistency models, strongest first
points: **Linearizable**: every operation seems to take effect at one instant between its start and its reply, so all readers see one order, in which an operation that finished before another started comes first. Chubby and Raft (lesson 11) give this.
**Causal**: if one write could have influenced another, every reader sees them in that order; concurrent writes may appear in different orders to different readers.
**Read your writes**: a client always sees its own earlier writes, whatever it sees of others' (lesson 4).
**Eventual**: if writes stop, all replicas reach the same value in time. Werner Vogels made the term widely known in 2008.

blocks.caption: Eight features of a social site and a shop, each needing a level of consistency. The weakest model that is still correct is the one to choose, since every step up costs latency or availability.

options.ask: Which is the weakest model this feature can live with?

items.name: Selling the last seat on a flight
items.why: Two buyers on two replicas must not both see the seat free; one order of operations is the only way to be sure.

items.name: A lock that one worker at a time may hold
items.why: Lesson 11: if two workers each read "free", both hold the lock.

items.name: A reply in a chat thread
items.why: A reply shown before the message it answers makes no sense; unrelated messages may arrive in any order.

items.name: Hiding an album from your manager, then posting a photo to it
items.why: The photo was posted after the change and because of it, so no reader may see the photo with the old access list.

items.name: Seeing your own new profile picture after changing it
items.why: You notice if your own change seems lost; others seeing it a few seconds late is harmless.

items.name: A comment you just posted, on your own screen
items.why: The writer must see it at once; other readers can wait for replication.

items.name: The number of likes on a post
items.why: A count a few likes behind for a few seconds harms nobody, and a CRDT counter merges it exactly.

items.name: The view count on a video
items.why: Approximate and late is fine, and counting must never slow down watching.

blocks.text: In July 2000 Eric Brewer gave the keynote at the Principles of Distributed Computing conference in Portland, Oregon, and put forward a conjecture: a shared-data system can have at most two of consistency, availability and tolerance of network partitions. Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch proved a precise version in 2002.[^cap] The usual summary, "pick two", misleads, because partitions are not optional: links fail. The theorem says what happens while one lasts. A replica that cannot reach the others must either refuse the request, giving up availability, or answer from what it has, giving up linearizability. Chubby refuses on the minority side; Dynamo answers and merges later.

Daniel Abadi pointed out in 2010, and in IEEE Computer in 2012, that the more frequent trade happens when nothing is broken. Waiting for other replicas before answering costs a round trip, often across data centres, on every request. His **PACELC**: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Dynamo and Cassandra are PA/EL: they answer during a partition and answer fast otherwise. Chubby and Raft are PC/EC: they refuse on the minority side and always wait for a majority.

Naming the trade-off for a feature means saying all three: the model it needs, what a partition does to it, and the latency it pays on an ordinary day. A like counter can be PA/EL with a CRDT and nobody notices. The last seat on a flight must be PC/EC, and the price is a slower purchase and, rarely, an error page.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on conflicts and consistency
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: One version of a key has the vector clock [A2 B1] and another has [A1 B2]. What should the store do?
choices: Keep [A2 B1], because A's counter is the larger one and A is listed first
Keep both: they are concurrent
Keep [A1 B2], because its last entry is the larger one and the last entry is the newest
items.why: Each clock is larger in one entry, so each version holds a write the other never saw.

items.ask: One version has the clock [A2 B1] and another has [A3 B1]. What should the store do?
choices: Keep [A3 B1] and drop the other, because it has seen everything the first one saw
Keep both and return both on the next read, since they differ
Keep [A2 B1], because the older version is the one more replicas hold
items.why: No entry of [A3 B1] is smaller and one is larger, so [A2 B1] happened before it.

items.ask: Why can last writer wins lose a customer's update without any error?
choices: It keeps every version but returns only the newest one, hiding the others until a repair runs
It refuses writes during a partition, so one of the two updates never reaches the store
It drops one of two concurrent writes, chosen by clocks that can be wrong
items.why: The dropped version is gone; if the clocks disagree, even the write that truly came second can lose.

items.ask: Dynamo's cart merged conflicting versions by taking the union of their items. What went wrong?
choices: An item added on one replica could be lost when the versions met
A removed item could reappear
Two copies of the same item were kept, so the quantities in the cart doubled after each merge
items.why: A union keeps everything in either version; only a record of the remove, as in an observed-remove set, keeps the item out.

items.ask: Which is a correct reading of the CAP theorem?
choices: A system must choose any two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance when it is designed
A system that is consistent can never also have low latency, even when there are no failures at all
During a partition, a cut-off replica must refuse requests or risk answering with stale data
items.why: Partitions happen whatever the design; the choice is what a cut-off replica does. The latency trade without partitions is PACELC's addition.

items.ask: Two editors type into one line at the same time, with no central server. What lets a text CRDT agree on the result?
choices: Every letter has a fixed id, and edits name letters by id instead of by position
A central server puts every edit in one order before anyone applies it
Each edit carries the time it was typed, and the later edit is applied last
items.why: An edit that names a letter means the same thing whatever was inserted before it; a central order is how Jupiter-style transformation works.

items.ask: Which feature needs causal consistency, but nothing stronger?
choices: The last seat on a flight, which exactly one of two buyers may get
A reply in a chat thread, shown to everyone in it
The number of likes on a post, which may lag by a few likes for a few seconds
items.why: A reply shown before the message it answers makes no sense, so cause must come before effect; unrelated messages may still arrive in any order. The seat needs linearizability and the like count only eventual consistency.

lamport.title: From relativity
lamport.text: Lamport has said the idea came from special relativity, where there is no single time for events in different places, only an order fixed by which events could have sent a signal to which. The paper also introduced logical clocks, single counters that respect happened-before, and used them to build a mutual-exclusion algorithm.

truncation.title: Clocks that grow
truncation.text: A vector clock gains an entry for every replica that ever coordinates a write to the key. Dynamo capped them: when a clock had more than about ten entries, the oldest was dropped, with a timestamp kept to tell which. A truncated clock can make two related versions look concurrent, which costs an unneeded merge; the paper reports that this had not been a problem in production.

tombstones.title: Cleaning up
tombstones.text: A remove's record must stay until every replica has merged the add it names, or a replica that has not heard of the remove could merge the add back in. Knowing that every replica has seen something needs the replicas to agree, which is the coordination CRDTs were meant to avoid, so real systems clean up rarely and in the background.

cap.title: What the proof means by each word
cap.text: In Gilbert and Lynch's proof, consistency means linearizable, availability means every request to a replica that has not failed gets an answer, and a partition means any messages between replicas may be lost. The theorem says nothing about weaker models: a system can be available during a partition and still give read-your-writes or causal consistency to clients that stay with one replica.

wave.title: Google Wave
wave.text: Google Wave, announced in May 2009, let many people edit a conversation at once, built on Jupiter-style transformation. Google stopped developing it in August 2010, but its engineers and its approach went into the collaborative editing that Google Docs gained that year.
